analysis.one_liner: Eliminates capital gains and estate taxes, opens the Arctic Refuge to oil drilling, and repeals disability and construction-wage protections.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to 10 House committees on July 8, 1992, scattered across a dozen subcommittees, and died without ever getting a vote when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This grab-bag bill would have wiped out federal taxes on capital gains and on estates and gifts, barred states from imposing inheritance taxes, and opened part of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to oil leasing with no further environmental studies. It would have handed oil and gas companies new tax credits and deductions, repealed the Davis-Bacon Act's prevailing-wage rules for federally funded construction, and repealed the entire Americans with Disabilities Act. It contained one clear benefit for working people: removing the limit on how much Social Security retirees can earn without losing benefits.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthy households would pay no capital gains or estate taxes. Oil and gas producers would get a 15% exploration credit, a credit on each barrel of marginal production, full percentage depletion without the taxable-income cap, and relief from the alternative minimum tax [S3]. Bidders would gain access to Arctic Refuge leases [S3]. Federal construction contractors would pay whatever wage they choose instead of the locally prevailing wage [S3]. Employers would be freed from all ADA accommodation and accessibility obligations [S3]. Retirees who work could keep full Social Security benefits regardless of earnings [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy families, oil companies, federal contractors

how_it_helps.text: Excludes net capital gain from gross income entirely, so profits from selling stocks and other assets would be untaxed [S2][S3].
Repeals the federal estate and gift taxes and bars states from imposing any inheritance tax, ending taxation of large wealth transfers between generations [S2][S3].

Gives oil and gas producers a 15% credit for exploration and drilling investment, a 15% credit on each barrel of marginal (stripper-well, heavy, or harsh-environment) oil, removes the 65% taxable-income limit on percentage depletion, and removes oil and gas preferences from the alternative minimum tax [S3].

Directs the Interior Department to open the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain to a competitive oil and gas leasing program, declaring an existing environmental assessment sufficient and requiring no further land-management review or studies before lease sales [S2][S3].
Repeals the Davis-Bacon Act, which required federally financed construction to pay locally prevailing wages, letting contractors on federal projects pay lower wages [S2][S3].
Repeals the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, applying federal law as if the Act had never been enacted, eliminating requirements for workplace accommodation and public accessibility [S2][S3].
Removes the Social Security earnings limit, allowing beneficiaries to earn any amount of outside income without a reduction in benefits, and makes a parallel change for railroad retirement [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The Treasury would lose the revenue from capital gains, estate, and gift taxes plus the cost of oil and gas credits, adding to the deficit — the bill's own subject list includes 'budget deficits' [S1][S2]. Disabled Americans would lose ADA employment and accessibility protections [S3]. Construction workers on federally funded projects would see pay driven down from locally prevailing rates [S3]. Alaska's Arctic coastal plain would be opened to drilling with the environmental review process cut off [S3]. Consumers would face the costs and benefits of a one-year freeze on new federal regulations [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Disabled Americans, federal construction workers, the Treasury

drawbacks.text: Repealing the Americans with Disabilities Act would strip away federal protections against disability discrimination and requirements for accessible workplaces and public accommodations, treating the law as if it never existed [S3].

Repealing the Davis-Bacon Act would allow contractors on federally funded construction to pay below the locally prevailing wage, cutting the pay of union and nonunion construction labor alike [S2][S3].

Eliminating capital gains, estate, and gift taxes while adding oil and gas credits would substantially reduce federal revenue, worsening the deficit — 'budget deficits' is listed among the bill's own subjects [S1].

The Arctic Refuge subtitle makes the bill the 'primary land management authorization,' waives any further land-management review or studies, and deems a pre-existing assessment sufficient, leaving leasing decisions with little environmental scrutiny before the first lease sale within a year of enactment [S3].

The reciprocal-trade subtitle would require the U.S. Trade Representative to restrict imports from any nation whose markets are not fully open to U.S. goods, a mandatory retaliation regime that economists widely expect to raise consumer prices and invite retaliation against U.S. exports [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundles a few popular ideas — repealing the Social Security earnings limit is a genuine benefit for working retirees — inside a package whose largest provisions are the elimination of taxes falling mostly on the wealthiest households and a large set of oil and gas tax breaks. Its costs are concrete and fall on identifiable groups: disabled Americans would lose ADA protections entirely, federally funded construction workers would lose prevailing-wage guarantees, and the Treasury would lose substantial revenue at a time of declared deficit concern. The Arctic Refuge provision would lock in drilling with the environmental review process deliberately cut short. The bill also covers the full spread of a serious governing agenda — tax policy, trade, regulation, disability law, labor law, campaign finance — in a single bill referred to ten committees, which is a design that makes serious consideration practically impossible.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 1992, referred to ten House committees and then farmed out to a dozen subcommittees, none of which acted, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Mickey Edwards of Oklahoma introduced the bill on July 8, 1992, with two Republican cosponsors [S1][S4].

The same day, it was referred to ten House committees: Ways and Means, Rules, Judiciary, Merchant Marine and Fisheries, Interior and Insular Affairs, Education and Labor, Energy and Commerce, Public Works and Transportation, Government Operations, and House Administration [S1][S5].

Over the following seven weeks it was referred to at least twelve subcommittees and Executive Comment was requested from the Departments of Energy and the Interior; no committee ever reported it and no vote was ever scheduled [S5].
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and the bill died with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the existing law stayed in place: disabled Americans kept ADA protections, federally funded construction workers kept prevailing-wage guarantees, and wealthy households and oil producers received none of the proposed tax cuts. No interest group gained anything from the outcome, but the groups the bill would have burdened were spared its costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Disabled workers and construction labor kept existing protections

against.name: House committees of referral
against.role: The ten committees (and their subcommittees) to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill among subcommittees and requested executive comments but never held a markup or reported it, so it never reached the floor

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Republicans, but the bill never reached a vote, so no record exists of how the parties would have lined up.

industries.note: The bill would grant a 15% exploration credit, a 15% marginal-production credit, unrestricted percentage depletion, AMT relief, and Arctic Refuge leases with no further environmental review. The revenue cost lands on the Treasury while drilling proceeds on a refuge that has otherwise remained closed.

Repealing capital gains, estate, and gift taxes would remove the federal taxes that fall almost exclusively on asset holders and large inheritances, with the lost revenue borne by the general treasury.
Repealing the Davis-Bacon Act lets contractors on federally financed projects pay below the locally prevailing wage, cutting labor costs at construction workers' expense.

industries.industry: Employers and public accommodations subject to the ADA
industries.note: Repealing the Americans with Disabilities Act removes accommodation and accessibility obligations, shifting the cost of disability access from businesses back onto disabled people themselves.

The bill would allow union employees to elect dues withholding for political purposes, but only if unions provide extensive annual notices, independent audits, challenge procedures, and escrow of disputed amounts — conditions that would restrict unions' political spending unless fully met.
